impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that claims directed to methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL invalidating Teva's headache patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache, after a jury had found willful infringement and no invalidity. The reversal reinstates a significant jury verdict in a high-stakes pharmaceutical patent dispute between Teva (Ajovy) and Eli Lilly involving biologics patent scope.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to obtain and enforce genus claims in the biologics space, particularly where the specification discloses known methods for making antibodies within the claimed genus, supporting broad patent protection for biologic drug developers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors and biosimilar developers face increased risk that broad method-of-treatment claims covering a genus of antibodies will be upheld, potentially limiting market entry for competing biologic therapies.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions using an emulator and a model of function calls are directed to an abstract idea under step one of the Alice framework for patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in allowing damages based on foreign sales.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the judgment, holding that Columbia's computer security patent claims were abstract at Alice step one and remanding for step two analysis. The court also held that the district court erred in permitting damages based on Norton's sales to customers outside the United States. The case involved a $185 million jury verdict including enhanced damages and attorneys' fees.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces limits on extraterritorial patent damages, protecting companies from liability for foreign sales in U.S. patent infringement cases. Provides clarity on the scope of Alice step one for software-related patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: University and software patent holders face heightened eligibility challenges for claims involving computer security and anomaly detection methods, potentially narrowing the enforceability of software patents in critical cybersecurity fields.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that has granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue third parties for infringement and other exclusionary rights retains sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain the right to sue for infringement—a right not rendered illusory by the license terms—possess a sufficient exclusionary interest to satisfy Article III standing. The court analyzed the license agreement's provisions on shared litigation control, sublicensing restrictions, and retained rights.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides patent owners with greater confidence that they can structure exclusive licenses while retaining litigation rights, enabling flexible licensing arrangements without forfeiting the ability to enforce patents against infringers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may find it harder to defeat patent suits on standing grounds where the patent owner has retained even limited exclusionary rights under a license agreement.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Insulet's Defend Trade Secrets Act claim was time-barred where the alleged misappropriation began more than three years before suit was filed, and whether Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation earlier.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict in favor of Insulet, holding that the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations had expired before Insulet filed suit. The court determined that Insulet knew or should have known of EOFlow's trade secret misappropriation more than three years prior to filing, entitling EOFlow to JMOL on the limitations defense despite the jury's contrary finding.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from a strict application of the DTSA's statute of limitations, particularly where publicly available information or industry knowledge should have put the plaintiff on notice.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face significant risk of losing claims if they delay filing suit, even while investigating, reinforcing the need for prompt action once there is reason to suspect misappropriation of confidential information.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that the plaintiff's asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known in the art can constitute inventive contributions for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict on trade secret misappropriation, holding that the plaintiff failed to prove its four asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed the patent inventorship finding, reasoning that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. The counterfeiting verdict and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides defendants with a strong basis to challenge trade secret claims where the allegedly secret information is generally known in the relevant field, reinforcing the requirement that trade secrets must derive independent economic value from their secrecy.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret plaintiffs must rigorously establish that asserted secrets are not generally known, as failure to do so can result in JMOL reversal even after a favorable jury verdict, including loss of exemplary damages and injunctive relief.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and the doctrine of equivalents, and whether the court improperly struck plaintiff's damages theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's grant of summary judgment of noninfringement of a multicore processor patent, finding genuine disputes of material fact on VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory. The court also reversed the striking of certain damages expert theories, finding the district court abused its discretion. The case was remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the court's willingness to allow doctrine of equivalents arguments and damages theories to proceed to trial, expanding opportunities to prove infringement of technology patents against major semiconductor manufacturers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies face continued exposure to broad patent infringement claims under the doctrine of equivalents, even where literal infringement is not established, increasing litigation costs and uncertainty.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for some patent claims relating to non-uniform constellation designs used in digital communications, while affirming eligibility for others. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on both non-infringement and damages. The decision creates a split outcome requiring remand on eligibility for certain claims while preserving the jury's infringement and damages findings for the eligible claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for claims with sufficiently concrete technical implementations, and the affirmance of damages findings supports robust enforcement of standard-essential patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing communication standards face continued patent exposure, while the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about the scope of patent protection for optimization techniques in wireless communications.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether the plaintiff was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no infringement of Actelion's patents covering epoprostenol pharmaceutical compositions, agreeing that the pH claim limitation refers to pH measured at a temperature standard in the field. The court also affirmed that Actelion was barred from asserting doctrine of equivalents infringement. This decision is significant for generic drug entry in the hypertension treatment market.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from clear claim construction standards for measurable parameters in drug composition patents, facilitating ANDA filings and generic market entry where the accused product's properties differ under standard measurement conditions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies may find it harder to enforce patents with measurable parameter limitations against generic competitors that can design around the claims by adjusting conditions under which the parameter is measured.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify outside of personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether the on-sale bar of 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that a prior art sale expressly disclose the device's internal functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the pre-AIA on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge, and that the on-sale bar does not require sales to expressly disclose a device's internal functionality. The court also held that source code is not hearsay because code commands are not 'statements.'
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from broader admissibility of 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony and a clear rule that commercial sales of devices trigger the on-sale bar regardless of whether the sale disclosed internal functionality, strengthening prior art defenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges based on sales of products whose internal workings were not publicly disclosed, and may face summary judgment based on corporate representative testimony from witnesses who were not personally involved in the prior art events.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it previously missed the deadline for seeking a stay of an earlier-filed action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the mandatory stay deadline under § 1659(a)(2) by dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action to obtain a new 30-day window. The decision prevents procedural gamesmanship in parallel ITC and district court patent litigation involving pharmaceutical products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders and ITC complainants benefit from certainty that respondents cannot manipulate filing deadlines to obtain mandatory stays of district court proceedings, preserving access to parallel judicial forums for patent disputes.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the § 1659(a)(2) deadline cannot cure the deficiency through refiling, limiting their ability to defer district court proceedings pending ITC outcomes and potentially exposing them to costly parallel litigation.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding the patent holder's damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report in a patent infringement case against Microsoft's Azure platform, and vacated the resulting summary judgment. The court found the district court erred in its application of Daubert standards to the expert's reasonable royalty analysis. The case was remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from a more permissive standard for admitting damages expert testimony, reducing the risk that meritorious infringement claims are dismissed at summary judgment due to overly aggressive Daubert gatekeeping.
impacts.negativeImplications: Large technology companies face increased litigation exposure as patent damages experts may be given broader latitude to present royalty theories, potentially increasing settlement pressure in patent disputes.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple Watch models incorporating blood oxygen measurement functionality infringed Masimo's patents and that Masimo established a domestic industry sufficient to support an exclusion order.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watch models that infringed Masimo's patents covering wearable blood oxygen measurement devices. The court upheld both the domestic industry determination and the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models, in a case with major implications for wearable health technology products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with established domestic industries in wearable health technology gain confidence that ITC exclusion orders can effectively block importation of infringing consumer electronics products from major manufacturers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics companies face significant import restrictions and product design constraints when wearable device features are found to infringe health technology patents, potentially requiring costly redesigns or removal of product features.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER operations, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary charged excessive PACER fees in violation of the E-Government Act. The court upheld the settlement terms providing full or substantial reimbursement to hundreds of thousands of PACER users, as well as attorneys' fees and incentive awards to the nonprofit class representatives.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses and law firms that are heavy PACER users will receive reimbursement of excessive fees. The decision validates the use of the Little Tucker Act for class claims against the government and affirms incentive awards to organizational class representatives.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its obviousness determination of challenged patent claims, including its analysis of the 'predetermined time delay' limitation in sensor-based logistics system patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination in an IPR of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent, finding errors in the Board's analysis of challenged claims relating to restricting access to shipment sensor information through predetermined time delays. The case also raised questions about third-party IPR petitions filed on the deadline of a party to underlying litigation. The matter was remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer appellate scrutiny of IPR obviousness determinations, particularly where the Board's analysis of specific claim limitations is insufficiently supported, protecting IoT and logistics technology patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on IPR to challenge competitor patents face uncertainty when third-party petitions are filed near statutory deadlines, and may see favorable Board decisions reversed on appeal for insufficient analysis.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss patent infringement claims with prejudice on obviousness grounds at the pleading stage based on an IPR determination against related claims, and whether the case qualified as exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of patent infringement claims as obvious at the pleading stage where related claims had been invalidated in an IPR, but reversed the § 285 exceptional case fee award and § 1927 sanctions against plaintiff's counsel, finding insufficient grounds for either. The decision clarifies the interplay between IPR outcomes and district court proceedings for surviving patent claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the ability to obtain dismissal at the pleading stage when IPR outcomes undermine related surviving claims, and the reversal of fee awards signals that merely losing a case on invalidity grounds does not make it exceptional.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with claims surviving IPR face risk that district courts may apply the IPR's reasoning to dismiss the surviving claims as obvious, even without full claim construction or discovery.
